summary: ASTRA (Astronaut Health and Environmental Monitoring System) is a proposed platform that brings together astronaut health monitoring, spacecraft environmental sensing, and selected psychological and behavioural indicators. It is built around NASA’s Human Research Program and its five hazards of human spaceflight: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and hostile or closed environments. It combines an ESP32-S3 microcontroller, biomedical and environmental sensors, Rust-based firmware, wireless communication, and a web dashboard. ASTRA is an engineering and research prototype, not a certified medical device or flight-qualified system.

ASTRA-H

Advanced Space Telemetry and Remote Astronaut Health Monitoring

PROFESSIONAL PROJECT REPORT  |  SYSTEM DESIGN, TECHNICAL ANALYSIS & VALIDATION PLAN

Version 1.0  •  15 November 2026

Project status: proposed research prototype; integration and performance claims require experimental verification.

Executive Summary

ASTRA-H proposes an integrated monitoring platform for astronaut physiological state, cabin conditions, radiation exposure, sleep, psychological wellness, and mission-defined navigation distance. An ESP32-S3 executes Rust sensor drivers, quality checks, feature extraction, configurable alert rules and telemetry packaging locally. Authorized clients consume timestamped measurements through a secure network service and view them in a responsive cyberpunk-style dashboard. The system is designed as a research prototype, not certified life-support or clinical instrumentation. Several peripherals remain unspecified; algorithms and sensor suitability require verification under realistic operating conditions.

1. Problem Statement and Objectives

Crew health data can be fragmented across devices, with different sampling rates, interfaces, and reliability characteristics. Delayed access, inconsistent timestamps, sensor dropout and overinterpretation of experimental psychological indicators create operational risk. ASTRA-H aims to consolidate measurements without implying that a single wearable can diagnose illness or infer emotion.

·        Acquire and timestamp biomedical and environmental sensor measurements on board.

·        Process raw signals in Rust with explicit data quality and sensor-health indicators.

·        Provide configurable alerts and historical trends, distinguishing missing data from normal readings.

·        Transmit authenticated telemetry to multiple clients, tolerating intermittent connectivity.

·        Keep driver, analytics, communication and UI modules independently testable.

2. Scope, Assumptions and Deliverables

In scope: an ESP32-S3-based breadboard or bench prototype, sensor abstraction interfaces, selected physical sensor integrations, onboard signal processing, telemetry, a browser dashboard, and repeatable test procedures. Out of scope: certification for crew medical use, vacuum/extravehicular qualification, direct interplanetary ranging, independent clinical diagnosis, and autonomous treatment. Position/range values must arrive from an external navigation source. Emotional-wellness indicators are exploratory and should incorporate voluntary self-report and human review.

3. Proposed System Architecture[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Figure 1. Layered architecture and external navigation dependency

Sensors connect over I²C, SPI, UART, ADC or digital GPIO as supported by the selected module. Rust tasks acquire readings and attach timestamps, sensor identifiers, calibration metadata and quality flags. Signal-processing components calculate features; rule engines generate alerts; a local ring buffer mitigates brief network outages. A communications service exposes versioned telemetry to an authenticated gateway or dashboard. The dashboard is a visualization client, not the authoritative calculation engine.

3.1 Data Flow and State Management

[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Figure 2. Acquisition-to-visualization data flow

Each observation should include measured_at, received_at, astronaut_id, sensor_id, metric, unit, value, quality, and sequence_number. Never interpolate missing measurements as though they were observed. Maintain a monotonic acquisition counter and synchronize clocks when a reliable time source is available. Configure sampling rates separately per signal and use bounded queues to prevent telemetry traffic from starving critical acquisition.

4.1 Electrical Integration Constraints

Use a common, documented power and grounding plan, level-shift incompatible logic levels, and avoid connecting medical electrodes to unsafe power configurations. The ADS1299 and AD8232 are measurement front ends, not complete medically isolated systems. Evaluate isolation, leakage currents, electrode protection, EMI, analog filtering and safe USB/power usage before human-connected testing. Do not assume every sensor tolerates the same voltage or spaceflight environment.

5. Software Architecture — Rust Workspace

A Cargo workspace should separate astra-core (shared types and validation), sensor-hal (interfaces), sensor drivers, signal-processing, environment, neuro-analysis, wellness, navigation, alert-engine, storage, telemetry and firmware-app. A separate dashboard frontend consumes the telemetry API. Compile firmware against the ESP-IDF Rust toolchain for the ESP32-S3; test pure calculation crates on a desktop target with recorded datasets.

5.2 Core Processing Logic

Use per-sensor sampling schedules; reject impossible values; retain raw data only where storage permits; apply validated filters and confidence checks; calculate derived features; compare against configurable thresholds; publish readings with provenance. Alerting must distinguish clinical thresholds from engineering demonstration thresholds. All derived values should identify their algorithm version and inputs.

6. Monitoring Subsystems and Analysis

6.1 Cardiovascular and Oxygenation

MAX30102 provides PPG signals for heart rate and estimated SpO₂. Motion, poor contact and perfusion can degrade both; oxygen saturation estimates require calibration and validation. AD8232 ECG enables waveform visualization and candidate beat detection; rhythm interpretation must not be labeled diagnostic without validation. A separate digital cuff or validated BP device supplies blood pressure; BP cannot be inferred reliably from these sensors alone.

6.2 Temperature, Cabin Atmosphere and Pressure

MAX30205 supports body-temperature trending. BMP280 provides an engineering prototype pressure reading, which can be converted from Pa to psi (psi = Pa / 6894.757). Oxygen concentration and total pressure should be considered together when evaluating oxygen partial pressure. MH-Z19B CO₂ results require environmental qualification and calibration; external temperature and dedicated pressure transducer interfaces remain to be selected.

6.3 EEG, Stress and Sleep

ADS1299 captures multichannel biopotential data; suitable electrode placement and reference design are essential. Rust can compute spectral power in frequency bands and quality indicators. Stress estimation is a research classification problem requiring labeled datasets, baseline normalization, subject-specific evaluation and uncertainty reporting. Sleep staging generally requires validated multimodal signals and cannot be promised from EEG-band heuristics alone. For isolation-related wellness, combine optional self-report with trends and avoid automated mental-health diagnoses.

6.4 Radiation and Navigation

Geiger pulses support counts per second or minute; converting to dose rate requires a characterized detector, calibration and radiation-energy assumptions. An accumulated count is not automatically a valid personal dose. The navigation widget displays an externally supplied Earth/spacecraft/anchor distance with units, source, age and confidence; ESP32-S3 alone cannot determine interplanetary location.

7. User Interface and Interaction Design[IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]

Figure 3. Conceptual cyberpunk dashboard widget layout

Use a dark navy background with restrained cyan/violet accents, legible high-contrast text and a clear warning hierarchy. Widgets: Heart & SpO₂, ECG, Blood Pressure, Body Temperature, EEG/Stress, Sleep, Wellness, Cabin Pressure, O₂/CO₂, Radiation, External Temperature, Anchor Distance, Connectivity and Alerts. Each widget should expose live reading, unit, timestamp, sensor status, recent trend, data provenance and an expandable detailed view. Critical warnings must use text and shape in addition to color.

8. Telemetry, Security and Multi-Device Sharing

For a bench prototype, ESP32-S3 can publish over Wi-Fi to a trusted gateway using MQTT or WebSocket-based messaging. A gateway can manage subscriptions, historical storage and remote clients. Adopt device identity, role-based access, TLS where supported, least-privilege permissions, replay protection, credential rotation and signed firmware updates. Distinguish local LAN transport from actual spacecraft-to-Earth communications, which require dedicated mission networking and can incur long delays. No assumption of continuous connectivity is appropriate.

11. Implementation Methodology and Phases

·        Phase 1 — Requirements: freeze measurable performance goals, interfaces, units, and hazard assumptions.

·        Phase 2 — Bench hardware: verify ESP32-S3 board, power, wiring, bus scanning and sensor self-tests.

·        Phase 3 — Rust firmware: implement HAL, drivers, structured readings, watchdog and local buffering.

·        Phase 4 — Algorithms: develop unit-tested feature extraction and quality estimation on recorded datasets.

·        Phase 5 — Dashboard: implement responsive widgets, histories, data-age states and alert controls.

·        Phase 6 — Connectivity: validate secure telemetry, reconnect, replay and multiple concurrent clients.

·        Phase 7 — Integration: run endurance, fault-injection, calibration and comparative measurement tests.

·        Phase 8 — Documentation: record results, limitations, bill of materials and reproducible build steps.

12. Verification, Validation and Expected Results

The following are proposed acceptance tests, not observed results. Record raw data, reference-device readings, firmware revision, sensor calibration, environmental conditions and test duration. Define numerical pass/fail thresholds only after requirements review and baseline measurements.

Expected outcome: a functional research demonstrator capable of collecting supported sensor data, calculating selected features locally in Rust, visualizing trends, detecting configured engineering events and sharing telemetry. Quantified accuracy, latency, uptime and clinical performance must be reported only after testing.

13. Cost, Schedule and Resource Planning

A defensible cost estimate requires exact sensor/module selections, sourcing quotations, quantities, power architecture, enclosure, PCB fabrication and calibration needs. The present design therefore uses a qualitative bill of materials rather than invented prices. Major cost drivers include ADS1299 acquisition hardware, electrode/isolation design, radiation detector calibration, optical oxygen measurement, digital BP integration and reference test equipment. Plan separate contingency for hardware replacement and compliance testing.

14. Limitations and Future Scope

Current limitations include undefined models for oxygen, external temperature, dedicated pressure, blood pressure and radiation; uncertain sensor suitability for reduced pressure or space environments; limited onboard resources; and unvalidated wellness algorithms. Future work could introduce higher-grade instrumentation, redundant sensing, secure time-series storage, validated anomaly detection, additional crew identifiers, mission-grade networking and hardware qualification. The path to operational use requires independent safety engineering and relevant medical/spaceflight approvals.

15. Conclusion

ASTRA-H offers a coherent architecture for consolidating astronaut physiology, environmental safety, experimental neuro-wellness and external navigation information. Its strongest engineering features are modular Rust computation, explicit measurement provenance, quality-aware alerting and synchronized multi-device telemetry. The design is technically suitable for staged prototype development, provided the remaining sensor choices, human-electrical safety, calibration and validation work are completed before any high-stakes use.
